stories.headline: Mehli Mistry steps down from Tata Medical Center trust
stories.title: Mehli Mistry steps down from Tata Medical Center trust
stories.summary: Mistry, a confidante of late Ratan Tata, informed the board of the medical center he will not seek a re-election upon the end of his term on September 30
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'steps down' in title weight 40
article_sentences: Mehli Mistry has stepped down as a trustee from the board of Tata Medical Center, Kolkata.
Mistry, a confidante of late Ratan Tata, informed the board of the medical center he will not seek a re-election upon the end of his term on September 30.
Other trustees on the board include Noel Tata and his children — Neville, Leah and Maya, as well as former Defence Secretary Vijay Singh.
The Tata Medical Center run by Tata Trusts is spread across 13 acres in New Town, Kolkata.
Established in 2011 it is an integrated oncology facility with over 400 beds.
Last October, Mistry had stepped down as a trustee in three key Tata trusts after board members voted against his reappointment.
Mistry subsequently has raised issues of governance and alleged misconduct by trustees before Charity Commissioner of Maharashtra.
The matter is expected to be heard on October 15.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders action against Mau SPs from 2023 over ‘casual approach’ in criminal case trial
stories.title: Supreme Court orders action against Mau SPs from 2023 over ‘casual approach’ in criminal case trial
stories.summary: A Bench said only two of 54 prosecution witnesses have been examined since charges were framed in a 2017 kidnapping case, calling the prosecution “absolutely slack”
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: 2 independent source groups -> high confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Taking strong note of the “casual approach” of the Uttar Pradesh.

Police in a criminal case trial, the Supreme Court has directed the State Government to initiate departmental proceedings against the Superintendents of Police who have served in Mau district since 2023.

A Bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R. Mahadevan noted that only two of 54 prosecution witnesses had been examined in the case, lodged in 2017, despite charges being framed against six accused in March 2023.
It noted that the 14-year-old son of the petitioner was kidnapped on September 27, 2017, and that neither he nor his remains have been found to date.

“This leaves us in no doubt that the prosecution, which is accountable for producing witnesses, has been absolutely slack in its duty towards the court in the conduct of the criminal trial,” the Bench said in its order of September 21, 2026.
The Court said it was primarily the investigating agency's obligation to produce witnesses.
“We are shocked at the conduct of the prosecution in not ensuring that witnesses are produced before the court for more than three years and, as of today, only two witnesses stand examined,” it said.
The Bench noted that, pursuant to its order of August 10, 2026, the incumbent Superintendent of Police of Mau was present in court and had filed an affidavit dated August 29, 2026.

"On a query of the court as to how many witnesses have been examined since charges were framed against all six accused, lastly on March 27, 2023, the answer is that two out of 54 prosecution witnesses have been examined," the Court said.
It noted that despite the framing of charges in March 2023, the prosecuting agency had shown not even a "semblance of seriousness" in getting the trial concluded.

“Accordingly, we direct the State of Uttar Pradesh to initiate departmental proceedings against the Superintendents of Police, Mau district, Uttar Pradesh, who served from 2023 till date, for such casual approach towards a duty cast upon them, especially in matters of trial.
The same shall be initiated within two weeks from today,” the Bench said.

stories.headline: ‘Need to work in tandem’: Telangana Chief Justice on trafficking, bonded labour
stories.title: ‘Need to work in tandem’: Telangana Chief Justice on trafficking, bonded labour
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
article_sentences: A five-year-old child trapped in bonded labour, families passing debt from one generation to the next, and survivors at risk of being pushed back into exploitation even after rescue were among the realities highlighted at a judicial colloquium in Secunderabad on Saturday.
Judges, police officers and experts stressed that rescue alone cannot end human trafficking and bonded labour; survivors also need sustained support to prevent re-exploitation.
We have to look at the larger picture and not just individual cases.
There is a need for convergence of all the departments involved,” Telangana High Court Chief Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh said.

The one-day judicial colloquium on ‘Human Trafficking and Bonded Labour’, organised by the Telangana State Judicial Academy (TSJA), with International Justice Mission (IJM) as its technical partner, brought together 255 participants from the judiciary, police, government departments, prosecution, district administration and civil society, along with technical experts and survivors.
The discussions repeatedly returned to what happens after a victim is rescued.
Without rehabilitation and sustained support, survivors can remain vulnerable to re-exploitation, while prolonged legal proceedings can force them to repeatedly relive their trauma.
TSJA president Moushumi Bhattacharya said bonded labour had no place in a civilised society.
“You cannot have men and women working for you for free without wages, let alone minimum wages.”
Telangana Police Academy director Abhilasha Bisht highlighted the intergenerational nature of bonded labour, saying families trapped in debt could pass the burden on to even toddlers.
For Divya Devarajan, CEO of Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty, the discussion brought back memories of one of her first rescue operations as a sub-collector in 2013.
Among those rescued was a five-year-old child trapped in bonded labour.
